Good morning.

Welcome to Macworld 2004. Thank you for coming this morning. You know, we've got over, I just checked, we have over 60,000 viewers connected with the broadband to the webcast right now, coming in from over 100 countries. So, uh, howdy out there. We got some fun things, we got some fun things to announce this morning, and uh, it's always hard for me to hear up here on stage. So if you guys could let me know how you feel about stuff when we announce it, that'd be great.

So, I want to start off with, uh, with this. This is called boilerplate. It's what we put on the bottom of our press releases and everything else. It's how we talk about ourselves. And, uh, it says, "Apple ignited the personal computer revolution in the '70s with the Apple II and reinvented the personal computer in the '80s with the Macintosh." And I want to focus on the second half and really focus on this, this word reinvented. Uh, it's hard for those of us, uh, there's some people in the audience who were born after 1984 here. So, it's, it's hard if you weren't there to remember, uh, how things were in 1984 when the Mac came out, which is 20 years ago this year. Um,

People, people were using command line interfaces. Uh, it was very weird. And the Mac came out and changed everything. Um,

With its graphical user interface, it was, it was literally a decade ahead of anything else. Uh, and it was a computer for the rest of us. Those of us who didn't want to learn computer ease. This is, I pulled the first brochure that we did, uh, from the Mac, and it was really startling that we had to go through and teach people like what a mouse was. Nobody'd ever seen a mouse. We made the world's first low-cost mouse and got it out there, and people thought, "What is that?" We had to teach people what pointing and clicking was, what cutting, copying, and pasting was. These were totally virgin concepts out there. And again, what people were used to was this strange thing. And they got used to the Mac pretty fast, even some developers we know. Uh,

And so, the hardware was also pretty miraculous for its day. It was the industry's first 32-bit processor. So Apple was the first company to bring 32-bit processing to the PC industry, and now we're the first to bring 64-bit processing with the G5. This was the original Mac team, uh, that did a lot of the work, a lot of the management.

And, uh, this, I kept these. This came from my own file because it kind of proves that we were once young. So, so that was the original Mac, and days before we introduced the Mac, we ran an ad.

We couldn't help ourselves. Hey, you know, today, uh, with us is Lee Clow, who is the driving force behind creating this original 1984 commercial. Stand up, Lee. There he is right there.

So, 20 years. This is the 20th year anniversary of the original Mac, and we're going to make something of this year. We are working on some incredible new products for this year. It's going to be a great Mac year. We've got some wonderful things that we'll announce throughout the year that I think you will love as much as we do. It's going to be a great 20th anniversary year of the Macintosh. Now, to start it off, we want to give you all our first 20th anniversary product, which is a poster. When the Mac originally revolutionized our industry, reinvented our industry, it did so because of the Macintosh operating system, the first graphical user interface. And Apple was 10 years ahead of the rest of the industry. Well, we're getting there again with Mac OS 10. We are now out ahead of the rest of the industry with the world's most advanced operating system again. Microsoft's copying us again. It feels great. And, uh, so Panther is the fourth major release of Mac OS 10 in three years. And of course, Mac OS 10's based on Unix. Panther has over 150 new features in it. We introduced it last year, and it's done great. Some of the features people love are Exposé. Uh, you know, we've made it really easy to run a bunch of apps. They're all protected. You can have a zillion windows open, but how do you find something? And now Exposé gives you a way to find it instantly. And we're finding that people are using this feature like crazy and really loving it. iChat AV, uh, text chat, adding audio chat, and now video chat to iChat. And we're finding people are using this like crazy. The new Finder has been very well received, uh, and I think it's the easiest to use Finder we've ever shipped. Fast user switching has been a real hit. And these are just a few of the features that we've added in Panther. And so what's it all added up to? Panther's been a huge success for us so far, and we now are, uh, we now have over 9.3 million active Mac OS 10 users, and that is approaching 40% of our installed base. 40%, which is huge. Let's take a look at how that's grown in the last two years. You can just see what it looks like right here. And we're going to cross 10 million active users this quarter. Now, what does this mean? What this means is we embarked on something really hard three years ago, which was to change our operating system. The last time Apple did that was in 1984, going from the Apple II operating system to the Mac operating system. We tried to do this three years ago, and you know what? We've pulled it off. The transition is basically now over. We made it.

This is not easy. Microsoft's done it once before when they went to Win 95, and they're going to try to do it again in 2000 and whatever with Longhorn. Uh, it is really hard and takes many years. This is the fastest operating system transition on record that we know of, where 40% of an installed base has moved over to a new operating system in three years. And we're very, very happy and very thankful. We now also have 10,000 native apps on Mac OS 10. And look at the slope of that curve. It's accelerating. And there's some neat new apps being announced here today. Uh, Bionicle from Lego and THQ, which is a great app is being announced here today. Macromedia is announcing a new version of Director MX, which is a really important app on top of 10.
